title: High-Engagement Searches with Inquiry Rates
prompt: Write a query that identifies saved searches with above-average inquiry rates. For each saved search, calculate the inquiry_rate as the number of inquiries divided by the number of properties matched by that search. Only include searches that have matched at least one property. Return searches where the inquiry_rate is strictly greater than the overall average inquiry_rate across all qualifying searches. Output the search_id, user_id, search_criteria, properties_matched, inquiries_made, and inquiry_rate (rounded to 4 decimal places). Order results by inquiry_rate descending, then by search_id ascending.
schema_ddl: CREATE TABLE saved_searches (search_id INT PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT NOT NULL, search_criteria VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL, created_date DATE NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE search_matches (match_id INT PRIMARY KEY, search_id INT NOT NULL, property_id INT NOT NULL, matched_date DATE NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE property_inquiries (inquiry_id INT PRIMARY KEY, search_id INT NOT NULL, property_id INT NOT NULL, inquiry_date DATE NOT NULL);

composite_moves: group by search_id to count properties_matched and inquiries_made
calculate overall average inquiry_rate using subquery
order by inquiry_rate desc, search_id asc

hints: You'll need to aggregate data from multiple tables to count both property matches and inquiries per search.
Calculate the inquiry rate for each search, then compare it against the average inquiry rate across all searches with at least one property match.

Use a subquery or CTE to first compute the inquiry rate for each qualifying search, then filter those with rates above the average using a HAVING clause or WHERE clause with a subquery that calculates AVG(inquiry_rate).
answer_key: WITH search_stats AS (SELECT ss.search_id, ss.user_id, ss.search_criteria, COUNT(DISTINCT sm.property_id) AS properties_matched, COUNT(pi.inquiry_id) AS inquiries_made, CAST(COUNT(pi.inquiry_id) AS NUMERIC) / COUNT(DISTINCT sm.property_id) AS inquiry_rate FROM saved_searches ss JOIN search_matches sm ON ss.search_id = sm.search_id LEFT JOIN property_inquiries pi ON ss.search_id = pi.search_id GROUP BY ss.search_id, ss.user_id, ss.search_criteria HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT sm.property_id) > 0) SELECT search_id, user_id, search_criteria, properties_matched, inquiries_made, ROUND(inquiry_rate, 4) AS inquiry_rate FROM search_stats WHERE inquiry_rate > (SELECT AVG(inquiry_rate) FROM search_stats) ORDER BY inquiry_rate DESC, search_id ASC;

_meta.scenario: a real estate listing platform tracking saved searches and inquiry rates
